story.title: Why this exists
story.p1: Every board comes with its own app, its own login and its own logbook. Climb a Kilter at your gym and a MoonBoard on holiday and you have two histories that never meet.
story.p2: Then one of those apps vanished overnight and climbers lost their logbooks with it. That is what happens when one company owns the only way into hardware you already paid for.
story.link: What happened, and how to get your data out

who.title: Who builds it
who.body: It started in 2024 with one climber and a repo, and it is still the kind of project people work on in the evenings. Bugs get found by someone standing at the wall, not by a QA team.

next.title: What's next
next.body: More boards, better offline, and getting your data out as easily as it went in. The roadmap is public and the arguments about it happen on Discord.

why.title: Why this page exists

why.p2: We promise not to enshittify Boardsesh, and self-hosting will always be an option. If you get something out of it and can spare it, chipping in keeps the lights on.

intro.title: Legal & Intellectual Property Policy
intro.p1: Boardsesh is a free, open-source, community-built alternative for browsing and interacting with standardised LED climbing training boards (Kilter Board, Tension Board, MoonBoard, and others). It is non-commercial and maintained entirely by volunteers.
intro.p2: We believe climbers should have the freedom to choose how they interact with hardware they've purchased, and that community-created data should remain accessible to the community.

facts.title: Climbs are factual data
facts.p1: A climb on a standardised board is a list of hold positions on a fixed, standardised layout (e.g. "start on A5, use B12, C3, D18, finish on K11"), combined with a grade and wall angle. This is factual, functional information — comparable to a chess position, a set of GPS coordinates, or a phone number — not a creative work of authorship.
facts.p2: Under U.S. copyright law, facts are not copyrightable (Feist Publications, Inc. v. Rural Telephone Service Co., 499 U.S. 340 (1991)). A standardised board with a finite number of holds (typically 200–500) produces climb definitions that are inherently constrained, factual, and functional.

community.title: The database is community-created
community.p1: The climb databases for these boards are almost entirely user-generated content. Individual climbers create and submit climbs. The board manufacturers did not author this content — they provide a platform for submission and display.
community.p2: The licensing position varies by manufacturer, but in no case does a manufacturer own the community's climb data:
community.aurora: Aurora Climbing (Kilter Board, Tension Board, and others): Aurora's Terms of Use grant them a "perpetual, unrestricted, unlimited, non-exclusive, irrevocable license" over user-submitted content. Crucially, this license is non-exclusive — it does not transfer ownership to Aurora, nor does it prevent the original creator (or third parties) from independently using, collecting, or presenting the same factual data.
community.moonBody: As of the last review of Moon Climbing's public-facing legal documents (February 2026), we did not find app-specific Terms of Service, an End User License Agreement, or a contributed-content license governing the MoonBoard app or its climb database. As with every board here, our position rests on the principle above: climb definitions are factual, functional data, and the databases are community-created.

compilation.title: Comprehensive databases have weak compilation protection
compilation.body: Even where a database arrangement might qualify for thin copyright protection as a compilation, the U.S. Supreme Court has held that protection extends only to creative selection or arrangement — not to the underlying facts. A database that comprehensively collects all user submissions without editorial curation (as these platforms do) is analogous to an alphabetical phone directory, which the Court found unprotectable in Feist.

attribution.title: Attribution & Respect for Creators
attribution.intro: We respect the climbing community and the people who create climbs.
attribution.item1: Where climb creator information is available, we attribute the creator by their username.
attribution.item2: We do not claim authorship of climbs we did not create.
attribution.item3Start: If you are the creator of a climb and would like it removed, please
attribution.item3End: or contact us and we will honour your request promptly.

interop.title: Interoperability & Hardware Compatibility
interop.intro: This project provides software and hardware designs that are compatible with standardised climbing board hardware. Climbers who have purchased these boards have a right to use third-party software and controllers with their own hardware.

software.title: Software interoperability
software.body: Our app communicates with board controllers over standard Bluetooth protocols. The Bluetooth communication protocol used by these boards is unencrypted and based on commodity hardware (WS2812B addressable LEDs driven by standard Bluetooth controllers). Implementing a compatible Bluetooth interface for the purpose of interoperability is well-established as lawful under both U.S. and EU law (Sega Enterprises Ltd. v. Accolade, Inc., 977 F.2d 1510 (9th Cir. 1992); EU Directive 2009/24/EC, Article 6).

controller.title: Open-source controller
controller.p1: This project also offers open-source controller hardware and firmware designs. The controller is an independent, original implementation that communicates using the same Bluetooth protocol as the official controllers. It is built on commodity components (standard microcontrollers and WS2812B LEDs) and does not incorporate any proprietary firmware, code, or hardware designs from any board manufacturer. No patents are known to exist covering the LED controller systems used by any current board manufacturer.
controller.p2: Our controller is designed to be interoperable with both this project's software and, at the user's discretion, official manufacturer apps. Any such interoperability is initiated by the end user on their own hardware.

trademark.title: Trademark Usage
trademark.body: We use board and product names (e.g. "Kilter Board", "MoonBoard", "Tension Board") solely to describe hardware compatibility and interoperability. These names are trademarks of their respective owners. This project is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Aurora Climbing, Moon Climbing, or any board manufacturer.

dmca.title: DMCA & Takedown Requests
dmca.intro: We take intellectual property concerns seriously. If you believe any material in this project infringes your copyright, please contact us with the following information:
dmca.item1: Identification of the copyrighted work you believe is infringed.
dmca.item2: Identification of the material you believe is infringing, with enough detail for us to locate it.
dmca.item3: Your contact information (name, address, email, phone number).
dmca.item4: A statement that you have a good faith belief that the use is not authorised by the copyright owner, its agent, or the law.
dmca.item5: A statement, under penalty of perjury, that the information in your notice is accurate and that you are the copyright owner or authorised to act on their behalf.
dmca.review1: We will review all valid requests promptly and in good faith. We may also file a counter-notice where we believe a takedown request is based on a misidentification of the material or a misunderstanding of the law.

community.title: A Note to the Community
community.p1: The climbing community has a long tradition of openly sharing beta. This project exists in that spirit. We are not trying to harm any company — we are trying to give climbers better tools to interact with hardware they already own and data they helped create.
community.p2: Manufacturers continue to benefit from this ecosystem. Our project drives demand for their physical products (holds, boards, panels) where they provide genuine value. We simply believe climbers deserve a choice in how they interact with their hardware.
community.p3: If you are a board manufacturer and would like to discuss collaboration or have concerns, we welcome open dialogue. Please reach out.

legal.footer: This document is provided for informational purposes and does not constitute legal advice. Last updated: 08-02-2026

hero.title: Help
hero.subtitle: This site is where climbs live on the web. The app is where you climb them. Here's what each one does.

web.title: On this site
web.intro: Everything here is a link you can send to someone. No install, no sign-in.
web.item1: Look up a climb and read its grade, setter and ascents.
web.item2: Browse a board's full catalogue by layout, size and angle.
web.item3: Share a climb, a playlist or your profile with a plain URL.
web.item4: Find a gym and see what's on its wall from the gym's kiosk screen.

app.title: In the app
app.intro: Anything that talks to the wall happens in the app.
app.item1: Build a queue and work through it with your crew.
app.item2: Run a party session so everyone's phone drives the same queue.
app.item3: Light up holds over Bluetooth on Kilter, Tension and MoonBoard walls.
app.item4: Log your sends and keep your logbook in one place.

aurora.title: Coming from the Aurora apps
aurora.intro: Boardsesh reads your existing account, so your sends come with you.
aurora.item1: In the app, tap your avatar and hit Settings. On the More screen that opens, pick Connected apps and hit Link next to Kilter or Tension. Your logbook syncs across.
aurora.item2: Your ascents stay yours. We never write back anything you didn't log.
aurora.item3: Sync runs one way. Your Kilter and Tension ticks come into Boardsesh; Boardsesh doesn't write anything back to their apps.

climbCounts.title: Why does Kilter's app show more climbs?
climbCounts.intro: Both apps have the same climbs. They just count them differently.
climbCounts.item1: Boardsesh counts each climb once and shows its grade and ascents at the angle you pick.
climbCounts.item2: Kilter's app counts a climb once for every angle it has been logged at, so a climb with ascents at 40° and 45° counts as two.
climbCounts.item3: That's why the same board can show up to about twice as many climbs in Kilter's app.

hero.title: Build a playlist and climb it in order
hero.subtitle: Stash your projects, pull the list up on board night, and take a climb back out when you're done with it.

build.title: Make a playlist
build.intro: Playlists live on the Discover tab.
build.p1: Pick your board first, then hit the plus on Discover. Give the list a name, a colour and an emoji and it lands under My Playlists. Climbs go in from the climbs themselves: swipe a row to the left, or hold it for a moment and choose Add to Playlist. The picker is a checklist, so one climb can go into several lists at once.
build.p2: Playlists belong to a board. The picker only offers the lists that match the board and layout a climb comes from, so a Tension list never fills up with Kilter climbs.
build.shotAlt: The Discover tab showing pinned playlists and auto-curated lists
build.shotCaption: Discover: pinned lists up top, yours below, curated ones after that.
build.playlistShotAlt: A playlist with its climbs and owner controls
build.playlistShotCaption: A playlist you own: pin it, edit details, reorder and remove.

remove.title: Take a climb back out
remove.intro: Yes, you can. Two ways, and one works from anywhere.
remove.p1: Fastest: open Add to Playlist on the climb again and tap the list that already has a check next to it. The check clears and the climb leaves.
remove.p2: From the playlist itself, open Reorder & remove climbs — the pencil in the playlist's own toolbar, or the row in the ⋯ menu. Every climb grows a red minus and a drag handle: the minus pulls it out after a confirm, the handle changes the running order. Done closes edit mode.
remove.p3: The curated lists further down have no edit mode, because nothing went into them by hand. Change what feeds them instead: un-heart a climb and it leaves Liked Climbs, log the send and it drops out of Projects.

queue.title: Climb the whole list
queue.intro: Tap any climb in a playlist and your queue becomes that playlist.
queue.p1: A tap doesn't just open the climb. The queue is replaced by the playlist in order, starting where you tapped, so swiping in the play drawer walks the list. If you had climbs queued after your current one, you get a Start playlist? check first and those climbs drop out.
queue.p2: In a shared session a tap is a look rather than a takeover — the playlist opens for you without moving anyone else's wall.
queue.sessionsLink: How a session shares one queue

smart.title: The eight lists you didn't build
smart.intro: Boardsesh keeps these running under For You.
smart.crowdFavorites: Crowd Favorites: the most-sent classics on your board that you haven't done yet.
smart.hiddenGems: Hidden Gems: highly rated climbs that haven't blown up yet.
smart.atYourLevel: At Your Level: climbs around the grade you've been sending.
smart.fresh: Fresh: new climbs from setters worth following.
smart.fiveStars: Five Stars: everything you gave five stars.
smart.mostRepeated: Most Repeated: the climbs you keep coming back to.
smart.projects: Projects: what you've worked hardest without sending.
smart.likedClimbs: Liked Climbs: every climb you've hearted.
smart.p1: Hearted a climb and wondered where it went? It went here. Liked Climbs is the list behind the heart on a climb row, and it's the fastest way back to something you spotted mid-session and meant to try later.
smart.p2: The first four read your board's whole catalogue at your angle and hold sets. The last four are built from your own ticks and hearts, so they fill up as you climb.
smart.p3: Tap the pin on a card to move it into Pinned at the top of Discover, where you don't have to scroll for it. Pinned playlists follow your account; pinned curated lists are per device.

tags.title: See which lists a climb is already in
tags.intro: Off by default, and worth turning on.
tags.p1: Tap your avatar, hit Settings, and scroll the More screen down to Display: Show playlist tags. Every row in the Climbs list that's already in a playlist grows an extra line carrying up to two small playlist chips and a +N for the rest, so you can skim a list and see what you've filed. Rows in no playlist stay as they were.
tags.p2: The chips are labels, not buttons — tapping one doesn't open the playlist. Leaving the setting off also stops the app looking up playlist membership while you scroll.

hero.title: Climb one queue with your crew
hero.subtitle: Start a session, share the link, and everyone's phone drives the same queue — without anyone's browsing moving the wall.

start.title: Start one
start.intro: The Record tab, and nothing else.
start.p1: Open Record, check the board at the top is the one you're standing at, and hit Start. That's the only thing that creates a session: your solo queue stays on your phone until you start or join one.
start.p2: Once it's live, Invite climbers opens a QR code with Copy link and Share under it. Show this session live also puts it in front of your followers and climbers on the same board; leave it off and the invite link is the only way in.
start.shotAlt: A live session with its crew and shared queue
start.shotCaption: A live session: who's climbing, what's queued, what's on the wall.
start.liveShotAlt: The Climbing now rail listing live sessions
start.liveShotCaption: Climbing now: live sessions you can join with one tap.

join.title: Join someone else's
join.intro: Three routes in, and no code to type.
join.p1: Whichever route you take, you land on the same card. It carries the host's name, the board, and how many people are on it, and nothing changes on your phone until you confirm. Already in a session? It asks before pulling you out of that one.
join.way1: Point your phone's camera at their QR code, or open the link they sent you.
join.way2: Climbing now on the Home tab, which lists live sessions from climbers you follow and from the board you're on.
join.way3: Climbing here now in the board sheet, which shows sessions already running on the wall in front of you.

queue.title: One queue, every phone
queue.intro: Anyone in the session can change it.
queue.p1: Add a climb and it shows up on everyone's phone straight away, with your face on the row so the crew knows whose pick it is. Anyone can add, drag to reorder, or pull a climb out: there's no host who owns the list. Ending it for everyone is down to the climber who started the session or whoever's leading it, and anyone else leaving just leaves.
queue.p2: If a phone drops off the wifi mid-session it catches up when it comes back and says so: the queue was out of sync, refreshed from your crew.

wall.title: Who's driving the wall
wall.intro: One phone holds the board, and it isn't a competition.
wall.p1: A board controller only lets one phone connect at a time, so whoever connects first keeps the link. Everyone else's lightbulb changes job: instead of trying to connect, tapping it asks the connected phone to light your climb. Nobody has to pass a phone around.
wall.p2: On a wall with no lights the bulb takes and releases the wall instead. Taking it tells the crew, and the gym screen, which climb you're on. If someone else takes it, yours is released quietly.
wall.p3: Commit while the wall is busy and you get a choice: someone just lit theirs, so put mine up or keep theirs.
wall.bluetoothLink: Connecting, and what to do when it fails

crowd.title: Four or five people in one session
crowd.intro: Browsing stops moving the wall the moment you're not alone.
crowd.p1: As soon as one other climber joins, swiping through climbs in the play drawer goes view-only. A Browsing pill appears at the top, and tapping it spells out why: you're just looking, the wall stays where it is. The lights only change when you use the commit row underneath. The app tells you once, the first time you join.
crowd.p2: Climbing alone and want the same thing? Hold the lightbulb and turn off Light problems on swipe and Light problems when tapping the list.
crowd.p3: So four people can flick through the catalogue while the fifth is pulling on, and nobody's holds go dark mid-burn.
crowd.previewLink: Preview a climb straight from the list

history.title: Sessions on your profile
history.intro: A different thing from a live session.
history.p1: Profile → Sessions is your climbing history: what you did, when, and how it went. Those are records, not rooms, and nobody can join one. They carry no share button either. The recap that goes out to Strava or Apple Health is the summary you get when you end a session.
history.p2: A live session is the one you start on Record. It's the only kind with a shared queue, an invite link and a crew.

hero.title: Find climbs by the holds they use
hero.subtitle: The Climbs tab does more than a grade range. Box off one corner of the wall, demand the crimp you want to train, or narrow a search to one setter.

start.title: Grade and angle first
start.intro: The two things that change the whole list.
start.p1: The Grade pill sits next to the search field. Tap a grade for a single grade; tap a second one within about three seconds and you get the range between them. Tap the same grade twice and it clears back to Any.
start.p2: Angle isn't a filter — it belongs to the board you're on. Change it from the degree control and grades, ascents and recommendations all re-read at the new angle. Boards with a fixed angle don't show the control at all.
start.p3: Signed in, the Progress chips do the thing people ask for most: Unsent hides everything you've already done, and Projects keeps the ones you've been working.

holds.title: Filter by hold
holds.p1: You get the full board, pinch and pan included, and you paint on it:
holds.step1: Choose Include or Exclude — must use this hold, or must avoid it.
holds.step2: Choose a type: Start, Hand, Finish, Foot or Any.
holds.step3: Tap holds on the board. Tap one again with the same brush to clear it.
holds.p2: A single hold can carry more than one type, so you can ask for a climb that starts on one hold and tops out on another. Clear all in the header wipes the lot, and backing out hands your picks straight to the filter sheet.
holds.p3: MoonBoard has no separate footholds, so there's no Foot brush. Start, Hand, Finish and Any are all still there.
holds.shotAlt: The hold filter with holds marked on a board render
holds.shotCaption: Tap holds on the board to say what they have to be.
holds.zoneShotAlt: A region box drawn over part of the board
holds.zoneShotCaption: Drag the box and its corners to pick a part of the wall.

zone.title: Box off part of the wall
zone.p1: Add a region drops a box onto the board. Drag the middle to move it and drag a corner to resize it. All holds keeps only the climbs that stay entirely inside the box, which is how you find something on a short wall. Any hold keeps anything that reaches into it.
zone.p2: Clear region takes it off again. Both this and the hold filter need a connection: on a downloaded board with no signal the app offers to clear them so you can keep browsing.

setters.title: Follow setters, then search only them
setters.intro: Two controls that do different jobs.
setters.p1: Follow sits on a setter's page, and on every row of Filters → The climb → Setters. Once you follow a few people, the switch Climbs by people I follow narrows the whole search to their climbs — no picking names each time.
setters.p2: The Setters screen is also a picker in its own right: tick boxes to filter the list to those names, or tap a name to go and browse everything they've set. Signed in, flip it between All setters and Following so you're choosing from a short list.
setters.shotAlt: The setters picker with checkboxes and follow buttons
setters.shotCaption: Check a setter to filter the list; tap the name to browse.

rows.title: What a climb row can do
rows.intro: Two swipes and a hold, on every list in the app.
rows.p1: Swipe a row to the right and the climb drops into your queue. Swipe it to the left and the playlist picker opens. Neither one lights the board.
rows.p2: The glyphs on a row are shape-coded, not colour-coded: a bolt means you flashed it, a circled tick means you sent it, a circled cross means you tried it, and a circled C marks a benchmark.
rows.p3: Holding a row opens the action menu, which is where preview, tick, share and the rest live.

keep.title: Keep the filters you use
keep.intro: Anything you reach for twice can live on the chip row.
keep.p1: Most sections in the Filters sheet carry a pin. Pin to shortcuts promotes that filter to the chip row above the list, so next session it's one tap instead of three.
keep.p2: The footer button counts the results before you apply anything, and Reset in the header clears the lot. Each climb counts once, not once per angle — which is why the number is smaller than the one Kilter's app shows.

next.title: Keep going
next.climbActions: What a long-press on a climb gets you
next.playlists: Save what you find into a playlist

hero.title: Log a send, then fix it later
hero.subtitle: Tick a climb in two taps from the board, and go back to change the grade, the stars or the note whenever you want.

log.title: Log it while you're at the wall
log.intro: The tick button in the play drawer is the fast path.
log.p1: The big button in the middle of the play drawer's action bar logs the climb you're on, and the queue bar has a Log ascent button that opens the same sheet. Date and time arrive already filled in; the rest is yours to set — your grade opinion, stars, how many tries, and a note. None of it is required.
log.p2: Two ways out of the sheet. Attempt records a go that didn't stick. The other button reads Flash when this is your first logged go on that climb at that angle and the tries are still set to one, and Send the rest of the time. Offline, or before your logbook has loaded, it stays on Send.
log.shotAlt: A climb lit on the board with the tick button below it
log.shotCaption: The tick button carries the climb's ascent count.
log.logbookShotAlt: The logbook list of logged ascents
log.logbookShotCaption: Swipe a logbook row for edit one way and delete the other.

edit.title: Change an entry you already logged
edit.intro: Including the grade and the stars you forgot at the time.
edit.p1: Your logbook is Profile → Logbook. Swipe a row to the right for the pencil, or hold the row and pick Edit logbook entry. A plain tap opens the climb instead, which is why this one hides. The edit sheet offers more than the log sheet did:
edit.field1: Status — Flash, Send or Attempt, so a send you logged as an attempt can be promoted.
edit.field2: Date, time, angle and how many tries it took.
edit.field3: Your grade opinion, your stars and your note.
edit.p2: If one row covers several goes on the same day, the app asks which entry you mean first.
edit.p3: Editing and deleting need a connection. Logging a new tick works offline and syncs when you're back; changing an old one has to reach the server.

delete.title: Delete one
delete.p1: Swipe a logbook row to the left for the bin, or open the entry and use Delete this ascent at the bottom. Either way there's a confirm, because it can't be undone.
delete.p2: A deleted ascent takes its comments and its votes with it, and your session and climb stats recount without it. A beta video survives: it stays on the climb and only stops pointing at that ascent.

repeats.title: Attempts, sends and repeats
repeats.intro: How a night at the board turns into rows.
repeats.p1: The default view groups by climb, day, angle and mirror, so four goes on the same problem this evening are one row with the tries added up and the best outcome of the day showing: a bolt for a flash, a tick for a send, a circle for a day it didn't happen. Climb it mirrored and those goes get a row of their own.
repeats.p2: Come back to it next week and that's a new row. Repeats stay visible instead of collapsing into one lifetime entry.

find.title: Find an old entry
find.intro: Search by name, then narrow it.
find.p1: The search field matches climb names. The filter sheet sorts by Latest or Hardest and narrows by status (sends, attempts or both), plus flashes only, a grade range, a minimum and maximum angle, a date range and benchmarks only. There's no board filter, because the logbook holds every board at once.
find.p2: Ascents you logged in the Kilter or Tension app come across with your account, so an old logbook doesn't get left behind.

next.title: Keep going
next.climbActions: Log a tick from any climb in a list
next.betaVideos: Pin a beta video to what you just logged

hero.title: Connect your phone to the board
hero.subtitle: What the lightbulb does, how to turn the lights off again, why one board shows up twice, and how to move through a session without picking the phone up.

connect.title: Connect
connect.p1: The bulb sits in the play drawer's action bar and in the top bar, and the small board chip next to the queue does the same job. Tap it and Select Board lists what's advertising nearby: a picture of each board, its name, its serial number, and three signal bars.
connect.p2: Pick yours and the app connects and lights your climb. The bulb fills whenever the wall is being driven, by your phone or by another phone in the session. The first time round, iOS asks for Bluetooth and Android asks to scan for nearby devices.
connect.shotAlt: The Select Board sheet listing nearby boards
connect.shotCaption: Select Board: nearest first, each row carrying its serial.
connect.litShotAlt: A climb lit on the board in the play view
connect.litShotCaption: A filled bulb means the wall is being driven, by you or by the crew.
connect.p3: Standing at a different wall? Change board is the first row of the menu behind your avatar, and the board capsule at the top of the Climbs list opens Now on the wall, which has Switch board at the bottom.

hidden.title: Hold the lightbulb
hidden.intro: The most useful control in the app is behind a long press.
hidden.p1: While your phone is connected, press and hold the lightbulb instead of tapping it. A sheet opens with the controls that have nowhere else to live, in this order:
hidden.row1: Auto-disconnect: after the idle time you set, your phone lets go of the board so somebody else can connect.
hidden.row2: Light the hold above: a dimmer LED over every lit start and hand hold. MoonBoard controllers only, so you won't see it on a Kilter or a Tension.
hidden.row3: Light problems on swipe: lights the board as you swipe between climbs in the play view.
hidden.row4: Light problems when tapping the list: lights the board when you pick a climb out of a list. Turn both of these off and browsing stops changing the wall.
hidden.row5: Re-light board: push the current climb to the LEDs again when a hold drops out.
hidden.row6: Turn off all lights: go dark and climb from memory without disconnecting.
hidden.row7: Disconnect board: the way out when you connected to the wrong wall.
hidden.p2: Disconnected, a long press does nothing. A short press connects instead.

failed.title: When it won't connect
failed.intro: Couldn't connect comes with the reason on it. Work down this list.
failed.fix1: Couldn't find your board. Make sure it's on and nearby, and if another phone is connected to it, disconnect there first.
failed.fix2: Couldn't connect. Move closer to the board and try again.
failed.fix3: Connected, but the board didn't respond. That one's the controller rather than the app: power-cycle it and try again.
failed.fix4: Bluetooth is off. Turn it on and tap the bulb again. Android also hides scan results until Location is allowed, and on Android 11 and older until the Location toggle itself is on. The picker offers the button for both.
failed.p1: Back out of the picker yourself and you get no message at all. That's a cancel, not a failure.

twoBoards.title: Two boards in range
twoBoards.intro: Tell them apart by serial, not by name.
twoBoards.p1: In a gym with two walls, both controllers advertise and both turn up. The list sorts by signal strength, but the bars are read once when a board is first seen and don't chase the signal while you stand there, so don't pick by bars alone. The serial on each row is the reliable one, and the board you used last is labelled Last connected board.
twoBoards.p2: Pick the wrong one and the app catches it: a warning says the controller belongs to another board setup, and offers to switch your setup rather than light climbs wrong. If you're already on the wrong wall, hold the lightbulb and disconnect.

duplicate.title: The same board listed twice
duplicate.intro: Almost always two boxes, not two names.
duplicate.p1: An Aurora controller advertises its name, serial and API level together, like Kilter Board#751737@3. A row that reads just Kilter Board with nothing after it is a newer, manufacturer-built LED box, not a second listing of yours. The picker keeps one row per controller, so two rows really are two boards: read the serials before you pick.
duplicate.p2: There's no forget-this-device list to tidy up, because the app keeps no list of Bluetooth devices. It remembers only the last board you connected to. Connecting to another one replaces it, and disconnecting on purpose clears it.
duplicate.p3: A duplicate in Your boards is a different problem with a different fix. On the boards screen, Edit next to Your boards turns the cards into management cards: a board you own gets Delete, one you only follow gets Unfollow. Renaming a board you own is the pencil on its card, with no edit mode needed.

control.title: When someone else has the board
control.intro: You don't need to take it off them.
control.p1: In a session, the bulb on every other phone hands your climb over instead of connecting. Tap it and the phone that's connected lights your climb. When there's nothing to hand over, the bulb just shows that someone else is driving.
control.p2: On walls with no lights the same control takes the wall: a virtual hold that tells the crew and the gym screen which climb you're on.

handsFree.title: Next climb without touching the phone
handsFree.intro: Chalk on your hands, phone on the mat.
handsFree.p1: On iPhone, a live session puts a Live Activity on the lock screen and in the Dynamic Island: the climb's name, its grade, where you are in the queue, and buttons for previous, next, re-light and, on boards that support it, mirror. It needs a session rather than a solo queue, and the navigation buttons appear on the phone holding the board.
handsFree.p2: Android gets the same controls as an ongoing notification, on the same terms. There's no headphone-button shortcut.
handsFree.p3: Either way the board link survives the screen going off and the app going to the background, so a session doesn't end because you put the phone down.

next.title: Keep going
next.findingClimbs: Find something to put on the wall

hero.title: Hold a climb to see what it can do
hero.subtitle: Every action on a climb lives behind a long press on its row — including a preview that shows you the climb without lighting the wall for everyone else.

open.title: Hold any climb
open.intro: It works on every screen that lists climbs.
open.p1: Press and hold a climb for a moment, in the search list, in a playlist or in your logbook, and the row lifts into a card with the climb drawn on its board. Three buttons run across the top: Log a tick, Add to Playlist and Share. Everything else is in the list underneath.
open.p2: If holding isn't your thing, the Climbs tab can put a ⋮ button at the end of every row, opening the same card. Turn it on from your avatar, then Settings, then Display on the More screen: Show quick-actions button.
open.shotAlt: The climb actions card open over a list of climbs
open.shotCaption: Hold a row: quick buttons on top, the rest of the list below.
open.previewShotAlt: The play drawer in its browsing state
open.previewShotCaption: Preview: the Browsing pill, and a commit row when you want the wall.

preview.title: Preview: look without committing
preview.intro: The first action in the list, and the least known.
preview.p1: Preview opens the climb in the play drawer without putting it in the queue. In a session, or with hold-lighting switched off, a Browsing pill sits at the top and a commit row waits underneath. Tap Set active when you actually want the wall, or Put on the wall if someone's climb is already lit. Climbing alone with lighting on there's no pill at all, and your next swipe hands the climb back to the queue and the LEDs.
preview.p2: In a session that matters twice over: your browsing doesn't light the board for the crew, and it doesn't reshuffle anyone's next climb. Someone can be mid-burn while you read the beta for the one after.
preview.p3: Climbing alone, the same thing is a setting — hold the lightbulb and turn off Light problems on swipe and Light problems when tapping the list, and nothing you look at reaches the LEDs.
preview.p4: Join a session and the app puts you in this view anyway.
preview.sessionsLink: How a session keeps browsing off the wall

quick.title: The three across the top
quick.intro: The ones you reach for between burns.
quick.p1: Log a tick opens the ascent sheet for that climb, so you can log from a list without opening the climb first. Add to Playlist turns the card into a checklist of your playlists, ticking to add and unticking to remove, without leaving the list you were reading. Share hands the climb to your phone's share sheet as a link.
quick.p2: The card closes itself once an action fires. Add to Playlist is the exception: it stays open so you can tick several.

rest.title: The rest of the list
rest.intro: What's underneath, and when each one shows up.
rest.queue: Add to queue: put it after your current climb instead of replacing anything.
rest.favorite: Toggle favorite: the heart, which is also what fills your Liked Climbs list.
rest.editEntry: Edit logbook entry: on a climb you've logged, opened from your logbook.
rest.betaVideo: Add beta video: signed in only.
rest.edit: Edit climb: your own climbs, while they're still a draft or freshly published.
rest.remix: Remix this climb: start a new climb from this one's holds, on boards you can set on.
rest.openInAurora: Open in Aurora app: for the boards that have one.
rest.report: Report climb: signed in only, and only where moderation is switched on. It sits last, because it's the one action against a climb.

next.title: Keep going
next.playlists: Playlists, pinning and the curated lists

hero.title: Pin a beta video to a climb
hero.subtitle: Share a reel straight from Instagram or TikTok, find the beta already sitting on a climb, and keep your own in one place.

share.title: Share a video into Boardsesh
share.intro: From Instagram or TikTok, using the share button you already use.
share.p1: Hit share on the reel and pick Boardsesh. The app opens on Attach your beta and asks you to tap the climb you sent it on, with your logged ascents underneath and a search field over them.
share.p2: When the caption carries the climb's name in quotes, Boardsesh reads it and lifts that ascent to the top under Matched from the caption, with everything else under Your other ascents. One tap attaches it — there's no second confirm and no way to unpin it afterwards, so check the climb before you tap.
share.p3: Instagram and TikTok links only; anything else is turned away. Boardsesh stores the link rather than the video, so the clip keeps living where you posted it.
share.shotAlt: The attach-your-beta screen listing recent ascents
share.shotCaption: Share a reel in, then tap the climb you sent it on.
share.shelfShotAlt: The beta videos shelf on a climber's profile
share.shelfShotCaption: Your beta collects at the bottom of your profile.

find.title: Find the beta already on a climb
find.p1: Open a climb and keep going past the board. Under it sit your logbook, the setter's notes, then a Beta Videos section with a row of clips pinned to that climb and the handle of whoever posted each one. Tapping a clip opens it in Instagram or TikTok — there's no player inside Boardsesh.
find.p2: If nothing's there yet it says so and invites you to be first. The plus in that section's header opens the same form as the menu action, so you can add yours from where you noticed the gap.
find.p3: Want only climbs that have beta? Beta videos only lives in the Filters sheet, and you can pin it to the chip row above the list so next time it's one tap.

add.title: Post one from a climb
add.intro: Share your beta walks you through it in three steps.
add.p1: Add beta video, from the long-press menu or the plus in the Beta Videos section, hands you a ready-made caption with the climb's name, angle and board already in it. Copy caption, then Open Instagram, and post the reel with that caption on it.
add.p2: Then send it back: share your own reel to Boardsesh, or paste its link into the field at the bottom of the same sheet. The caption is what lets Boardsesh tie the reel to the climb, which is why it's step one.
add.p3: There's no start time and no description to fill in. The climb, the board and the angle all come from wherever you opened it.

shelf.title: Your own beta
shelf.intro: At the bottom of your profile's Progress tab.
shelf.p1: Everything you've pinned collects in a Beta videos shelf under your stats and charts, with See all for the full grid. Other climbers' shelves work the same way on their profiles, and a climber with no beta simply has no shelf.
shelf.p2: Adding beta needs an account. Reading it doesn't — send someone a climb link and they'll see its beta without signing in.

overview.title: Boardsesh API Overview
overview.intro: Boardsesh provides two complementary APIs for interacting with interactive climbing training boards (Kilter, Tension):

rest.title: REST API
rest.intro: Use the REST API for stateless operations like searching climbs, fetching board configuration, and user authentication. The REST API is ideal for:
rest.feature4: Resolving URL slugs to numeric IDs

ws.title: WebSocket GraphQL API
ws.intro: Use the WebSocket API for real-time features like party sessions and queue synchronization. The GraphQL API provides:
ws.feature4: All REST API functionality via queries/mutations

auth.title: Authentication
auth.restBody: Uses NextAuth session cookies. Authenticate via
auth.wsBodyEnd: and include it in the connection parameters:

rateLimit.title: Rate Limiting
rateLimit.body: Authentication endpoints are rate-limited to prevent abuse. Rate limit headers are included in responses. Public read endpoints have generous limits.

ws.title: WebSocket Connection Guide
ws.introStart: The Boardsesh WebSocket API uses the

session.title: Session Management
session.body: Sessions are the core collaboration unit. Users join sessions to share a climb queue.

delta.title: Delta Synchronization
delta.body: When reconnecting, use delta sync to catch up without full state transfer:

connectionHandling.title: Connection Handling
connectionHandling.body: The WebSocket connection may be interrupted by network changes. Implement reconnection logic with the graphql-ws retry options and use delta sync to maintain state consistency.

privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.intro1: Boardsesh is an open-source app for controlling climbing training boards (Kilter, Tension, MoonBoard) over Bluetooth. This policy explains what data we collect, why, and what we do with it.
privacy.intro2ProductAnalytics: The short version: we collect only what we need to make the app work. We do not sell your data, we do not run ads, and we do not share data with third-party marketers or data brokers.

collect.title: What we collect
collect.accountBody: When you create an account, we store your email address and username. Your email is used for authentication. Your username is displayed on your profile and visible to other users in Party Mode sessions and social features.
collect.activityBody: When you log a send or attempt, we store the climb details, grade, date, and any notes you add. This powers your logbook and progression tracking.
collect.locationBody: If you grant location permission, we use your approximate location to help you discover nearby Party Mode sessions. We do not track your location in the background or store location history.
collect.productAnalyticsBody: We use PostHog and Vercel Analytics to understand feature usage, page views, performance, and where the app is slow. Some signed-in product events are linked to your Boardsesh account so we can understand which features are useful. We do not use this data for ads.

bluetooth.title: Bluetooth
bluetooth.body: Boardsesh uses Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) to connect to your climbing board's LED controller. The Bluetooth connection is used exclusively to send hold lighting commands to the board. No personal data is transmitted over Bluetooth. The app does not read data from the board beyond basic device identification during pairing.

location.title: Location data
location.body1: Location access is optional. When granted, it is used for one purpose: making your Party Mode session discoverable to nearby climbers. Your location is shared with the server only while a Party Mode session is active. We do not store your location history, build a location profile, or share location data with anyone outside of the party session discovery feature.
location.body2: You can revoke location permission at any time in your device settings. The app works fully without it.

thirdParty.title: Third-party services
thirdParty.vercelBody: We use Vercel for hosting and analytics. Vercel processes requests to serve the app and collects anonymous usage metrics. See
thirdParty.posthogBody: We use PostHog for product analytics, including server-side events for native app features like iOS Live Activities. See
thirdParty.auroraBody: If you link your Aurora Climbing account (used by Kilter and Tension boards), we sync your climb data with Aurora's servers so your logbook stays consistent across apps. This sync only happens when you initiate it. See

sharing.title: Data sharing
sharing.body1ProductAnalytics: We do not sell your data. We do not run ads. We do not share your information with third-party marketers or data brokers. The only data shared externally is what is described above (Vercel hosting/analytics, PostHog product analytics, Aurora Climbing sync when you opt in).
sharing.body2: Other Boardsesh users can see your username, profile, and logged climbs if you participate in social features like Party Mode. This is visible in the app and is part of how the product works.

retention.title: Data retention
retention.body: We keep your account data and climb history for as long as your account is active. If you stop using Boardsesh, your data stays until you delete your account.

deletion.title: Account deletion
deletion.intro: You can delete your account and all associated data at any time. There are two ways to do it:
deletion.inAppBody: Open More from your profile, scroll to the bottom, and tap Delete Account. You will be asked to confirm before anything is removed.
deletion.onWebBodyEnd: and open More from your profile to find the same Delete Account button.
deletion.permanent: Deletion is immediate and permanent. Once confirmed, we remove your email address, username, logbook entries, queue data, and party session history from our servers. This cannot be undone.

children.title: Children
children.body: Boardsesh is not directed at children under 13. We do not knowingly collect personal information from children under 13. If you believe a child under 13 has created an account, contact us and we will delete it.

changes.title: Changes to this policy
changes.body: If we change this privacy policy, we will update this page with the new text and the "last updated" date. For significant changes, we may also notify you in the app.

contact.title: Contact
contact.body1Start: Questions about this policy or your data? Email us at
contact.body2Start: Boardsesh is open source. You can see exactly what data the app collects and how it is processed by reading the source code on
